**Problem A1: Shake It**
Most hairy mammals shake after getting wet; shaking the water off is energetically advantageous to waiting for it to dry on its own. In this problem, we investigate the mechanics of shaking off water. For simplicity, we will model animals as solid cylinders with the sides covered in fur. You may ignore gravity throughout the problem.

a. We can model the shaking by assuming that the angular position of the cylinder undergoes a sinusoidal oscillation: θ = A cos(ωt). (The rotation is about the axis of rotational symmetry.) Letting the radius of the cylindrical animal be R, derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of a point on the surface of the animal under such a motion.

b. For the rest of this problem, rather than modeling sinusoidal motion, we will assume that the cylindrical animal is simply spinning at constant angular speed ω. Wet fur tends to separate into cylindrical clumps of radius r ≪ R. A droplet of water on the end of a clump of fur will be separated from it if the centripetal force overcomes the forces due to surface tension. Derive an approximate relationship (valid up to scalar numerical constants) between the surface tension σ, the radius r of the fur clump, the radius R of the animal, the angular speed ω, and the density ρ of water. The diagram below show the cross-section of the animal, showing four clumps of fur with droplets on their end.
[Diagram description: A large circle representing the cross-section of the cylindrical animal. On the right side of the circle, four small, closely spaced cylindrical clumps of fur protrude radially outward. Each clump has a small hemispherical droplet of water at its outer end.]

c. Experimentally, it is observed that all mammalian fur forms clumps of similar radius. Under the assumption that different animals all have the same density and are simply scaled copies of each other (i.e. larger animals are both longer and fatter), the relationship between an animal’s mass M and its angular velocity of shaking ω is of the form ω ∼ M^n: find the value of n.

d. Shaking requires energy, which we can crudely model as the rotational energy of the corresponding cylinder. An alternative strategy for the animal is to simply air-dry their fur, which requires energy to evaporate the water. Assume a wet animal has approximately 5% of their body weight in water, and has to supply all the energy for evaporating the water. Our model predicts that for some animal sizes, it will be energetically advantageous to air dry themselves: estimate the range of animal masses for which this is true. You may use the following facts: a mouse weighs 20 g, has a radius of 1 cm, and shakes itself with angular velocity ω = 30 rad/s. The latent heat of vaporization of water at room temperature is λ = 2430 J/g.

**Part a**
Let the angular position of the cylinder be $\theta(t) = A \cos(\omega t)$. The position of a point on the surface of the animal in polar coordinates is $(R, \theta(t))$. 
The angular velocity and angular acceleration of the point are:
$$\dot{\theta}(t) = -A\omega \sin(\omega t)$$
$$\ddot{\theta}(t) = -A\omega^2 \cos(\omega t)$$
The acceleration of a point in circular motion has two perpendicular components: the tangential acceleration $a_t$ and the radial (centripetal) acceleration $a_r$.
$$a_t = R\ddot{\theta} = -RA\omega^2 \cos(\omega t)$$
$$a_r = -R\dot{\theta}^2 = -RA^2\omega^2 \sin^2(\omega t)$$
The magnitude of the total acceleration $a$ is the vector sum of these components:
$$a = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_r^2} = \sqrt{R^2 A^2 \omega^4 \cos^2(\omega t) + R^2 A^4 \omega^4 \sin^4(\omega t)}$$
$$a = RA\omega^2 \sqrt{\cos^2(\omega t) + A^2 \sin^4(\omega t)}$$

**Part b**
We model the droplet of water at the end of the fur clump as a hemisphere (or sphere) of radius $r$. Its mass is proportional to its volume and the density of water:
$$m \sim \rho r^3$$
The droplet is moving in a circle of radius approximately $R$ (since $r \ll R$) at a constant angular speed $\omega$. The centripetal force required to keep the droplet attached is:
$$F_c = m\omega^2 R \sim \rho r^3 \omega^2 R$$
This force is provided by the surface tension $\sigma$ acting along the perimeter of the fur clump's cross-section (which has circumference $2\pi r \sim r$). The surface tension force is:
$$F_s \sim \sigma r$$
The droplet separates when the centripetal force overcomes the surface tension ($F_c \sim F_s$):
$$\rho r^3 \omega^2 R \sim \sigma r \implies \sigma \sim \rho r^2 \omega^2 R$$

**Part c**
From the relationship derived in Part b, we can isolate $\omega^2$:
$$\omega^2 \sim \frac{\sigma}{\rho r^2 R}$$
We are given that for all mammals, the fur clump radius $r$ is roughly constant. The surface tension $\sigma$ and water density $\rho$ are also constants. Therefore, we have:
$$\omega^2 \sim R^{-1}$$
Because the animals are modeled as scaled copies of each other with the same uniform density, their mass $M$ scales with the volume, meaning $M \sim R^3$, or equivalently $R \sim M^{1/3}$. Substituting this into our proportionality for $\omega^2$:
$$\omega^2 \sim (M^{1/3})^{-1} = M^{-1/3} \implies \omega \sim M^{-1/6}$$
Thus, the value of $n$ is **$-1/6$**.

**Part d**
We are asked to find the range of masses where the energy required to shake is greater than the energy required to air-dry (evaporate the water).
The energy to air-dry is the latent heat of vaporization for the water on the animal. The mass of the water is $5\%$ of the animal's mass ($m_w = 0.05M$).
$$E_{\text{evap}} = m_w \lambda = 0.05 M \lambda$$
The energy of shaking is crudely modeled as the rotational kinetic energy of the solid cylindrical animal ($I = \frac{1}{2}MR^2$):
$$E_{\text{shake}} = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{1}{4}MR^2\omega^2$$
Air-drying becomes energetically advantageous when $E_{\text{shake}} > E_{\text{evap}}$:
$$\frac{1}{4}MR^2\omega^2 > 0.05 M \lambda \implies R^2\omega^2 > 0.2\lambda$$
From Part c, we know that $\omega^2 R$ is a constant across all animals. We can evaluate this constant using the given properties of a mouse ($R_0 = 0.01$ m, $\omega_0 = 30$ rad/s):
$$\omega^2 R = \omega_0^2 R_0 = (30)^2(0.01) = 9 \text{ m/s}^2$$
Substitute $\omega^2 = \frac{9}{R}$ into our inequality:
$$R^2 \left(\frac{9}{R}\right) > 0.2\lambda \implies 9R > 0.2\lambda$$
Using the latent heat of vaporization $\lambda = 2430 \text{ J/g} = 2.43 \times 10^6 \text{ J/kg}$:
$$9R > 0.2(2.43 \times 10^6) \implies 9R > 4.86 \times 10^5 \implies R > 54,000 \text{ m}$$
Finally, we scale the mass of the mouse ($M_0 = 0.02$ kg) up to this threshold radius using $M \propto R^3$:
$$M > M_0 \left(\frac{R}{R_0}\right)^3 = 0.02 \left(\frac{54,000}{0.01}\right)^3 = 0.02(5.4 \times 10^6)^3 \approx 3.15 \times 10^{18} \text{ kg}$$
*(Note: While this mass is on the scale of a small asteroid and biologically impossible, it is the strict mathematical consequence of the scaling model provided).*

**Range of animal masses:** $M \gtrsim 3.15 \times 10^{18} \text{ kg}$

Problem A2: Black Tides

Consider a spherically symmetric, nonrotating star of mass $m$ and radius $r$. If it gets too close to the supermassive black hole of mass $M \gg m$ at the center of a galaxy, it will be ripped apart by tidal forces. Throughout this problem, neglect relativistic effects and give answers in terms of $G$, $M$, $m$, and $r$. When asked for numbers, assume the star is Sun-like, so that $m = 2 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$, $r = 7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}$, and $M = 10^6 m$, and give all numeric answers to one significant figure.

a. Suppose the star orbits the black hole in a circle of radius $R$. What is the radius of curvature of the trajectory of each point on the star's surface? Note that the star does not rotate as it orbits.

b. Gas on the star's surface facing the black hole is attracted to the star by the star's gravity, and pulled away from the star by the black hole's tidal force. Write an expression for the tidal acceleration at the point closest to the black hole.

c. At a radius $R$ where the gravitational and tidal forces are in equilibrium, the star will start being tidally ripped apart. This effect can only be observed when $R$ is outside the black hole's Schwarzschild radius $R_s = 2GM/c^2$. Find an expression for $R$ and numerically evaluate the ratio $R/R_s$.

For the rest of the problem, we consider a star on a parabolic orbit whose periapsis (distance of closest approach) is equal to the radius $R$ found in part c. Near periapsis, the star will be torn apart in a “tidal disruption event”. As a very rough model of this phenomenon, assume the star is initially a single rigid body. The moment it reaches periapsis, it fragments into many rigid pieces which do not interact with other, and feel only the black hole's gravity.

d. Afterward, some of the fragments will escape from the black hole, while the rest remain bound. Numerically evaluate the fraction of the mass which escapes.

e. An escaping fragment has speed $v_f$ when it is far from the black hole. Find the maximum possible value of $v_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

f. A bound fragment orbits with period $T_f$. Find the minimum possible value of $T_f$, among all fragments, and evaluate it numerically.

As bound fragments return to the location of the initial disruption, they collide with other debris, causing them to be absorbed into the black hole's accretion disk. This process produces an enormous amount of light, with the luminosity (or energy emitted over time) proportional to the mass absorption rate. If $t = 0$ at the moment the star fragments apart, then light begins to be emitted at the time you found in part f, and afterward the luminosity scales as $L \propto 1/t^n$ for a constant $n$.

g. Find the value of $n$. Assume for simplicity that the total energies of the bound fragments are uniformly distributed between their minimum and maximum values.
turns.official_answer:
a. $R$
b. $\frac{2GMr}{R^3}$
c. $R = r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$, $R/R_s = 30$
d. $0.5$
e. $v_f = \left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/6} \sqrt{\frac{Gm}{r}} = 5 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$
f. $T_f = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{r^3}{2Gm}} \sqrt{\frac{M}{m}} = 7 \times 10^6 \text{ s} = 80 \text{ days}$
g. $n = 5/3$

**Part a**
Since the star does not rotate as it orbits, its orientation remains fixed relative to the distant stars. This means that every point on the star undergoes the exact same translational motion as the center of the star, just shifted by a constant displacement vector. Because the center of the star moves in a circle of radius $R$, the trajectory of every point on the star's surface is also a circle of radius $R$. 
**Radius of curvature:** $R$

**Part b**
The gravitational acceleration due to the black hole at the center of the star is $a_c = \frac{GM}{R^2}$. The acceleration at the point on the star's surface closest to the black hole (a distance $R-r$ from the black hole) is $a_p = \frac{GM}{(R-r)^2}$. The tidal acceleration is the difference between these two:
$$a_{\text{tidal}} = a_p - a_c = \frac{GM}{(R-r)^2} - \frac{GM}{R^2}$$
Since $r \ll R$, we can use the first-order binomial expansion $(1 - r/R)^{-2} \approx 1 + 2r/R$:
$$a_{\text{tidal}} \approx \frac{GM}{R^2} \left(1 + \frac{2r}{R}\right) - \frac{GM}{R^2} = \frac{2GMr}{R^3}$$
**Tidal acceleration:** $\frac{2GMr}{R^3}$

**Part c**
The star begins to be ripped apart when the tidal acceleration equals the star's own surface gravitational acceleration, $\frac{Gm}{r^2}$:
$$\frac{Gm}{r^2} = \frac{2GMr}{R^3} \implies R^3 = \frac{2Mr^3}{m} \implies R = r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$$
To find the ratio $R/R_s$, we first calculate $R$ and $R_s$:
$$R = (7 \times 10^8 \text{ m}) \left(\frac{2 \times 10^6 m}{m}\right)^{1/3} = (7 \times 10^8)(126) \approx 8.8 \times 10^{10} \text{ m}$$
$$R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2} = \frac{2(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{36})}{(3 \times 10^8)^2} \approx 3.0 \times 10^9 \text{ m}$$
The ratio is $R/R_s \approx \frac{8.8 \times 10^{10}}{3.0 \times 10^9} \approx 29.3$. To one significant figure, this is $30$.
**Expression for $R$:** $r\left(\frac{2M}{m}\right)^{1/3}$
**Ratio $R/R_s$:** $3 \times 10^1$ (or $30$)

**Part d**
At periapsis, the star is moving at velocity $v_0 = \sqrt{2GM/R}$. Because the star is a non-rotating rigid body prior to disruption, all fragments initially share this velocity. The specific orbital energy of a fragment at a distance $x$ from the star's center (where positive $x$ points away from the black hole) is:
$$\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}v_0^2 - \frac{GM}{R+x} = \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{R(1+x/R)} \approx \frac{GM}{R} - \frac{GM}{R}\left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right) = \frac{GMx}{R^2}$$
Fragments with $\epsilon > 0$ (which corresponds to $x > 0$) will escape. Because the star is spherically symmetric, exactly half of its mass lies in the hemisphere $x > 0$.
**Fraction of mass which escapes:** $0.5$

**Part e**
The escaping fragments have specific energy $\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}v_f^2$. The maximum energy corresponds to the maximum distance from the center, $x = r$. 
$$\frac{1}{2}v_{f,\text{max}}^2 = \frac{GMr}{R^2} \implies v_{f,\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{R^2}}$$
Substituting $R = r(2M/m)^{1/3}$:
$$v_{f,\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GMr}{r^2 (2M/m)^{2/3}}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \left(\frac{2m}{M}\right)^{1/3}$$
Evaluating this numerically:
$$v_{f,\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{36})}{7 \times 10^8}} \left(2 \times 10^{-6}\right)^{1/3} \approx 4.9 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$$
To one significant figure, this is $5 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$.
**Maximum $v_f$ expression:** $\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} \left(\frac{2m}{M}\right)^{1/3}$
**Maximum $v_f$ numeric:** $5 \times 10^6 \text{ m/s}$

**Part f**
Bound fragments have $\epsilon < 0$. The minimum period $T_f$ corresponds to the most tightly bound fragment, which has the most negative energy (at $x = -r$): $\epsilon_{\text{min}} = -\frac{GMr}{R^2}$.
The semi-major axis is $a_{\text{min}} = \frac{GM}{2|\epsilon_{\text{min}}|} = \frac{R^2}{2r}$. Using Kepler's Third Law:
$$T_{\text{min}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a_{\text{min}}^3}{GM}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{R^6}{8r^3 GM}}$$
Substituting $R^6 = r^6 (2M/m)^2 = 4M^2 r^6 / m^2$:
$$T_{\text{min}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{4M^2 r^6 / m^2}{8r^3 GM}} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{2Mr^3}{Gm^2}}$$
Evaluating this numerically:
$$T_{\text{min}} = \pi \sqrt{\frac{2(2 \times 10^{36})(7 \times 10^8)^3}{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(2 \times 10^{30})^2}} \approx 7.1 \times 10^6 \text{ s}$$
To one significant figure, this is $7 \times 10^6 \text{ s}$.
**Minimum $T_f$ expression:** $\pi \sqrt{\frac{2Mr^3}{Gm^2}}$
**Minimum $T_f$ numeric:** $7 \times 10^6 \text{ s}$

**Part g**
The period of a bound fragment depends on its specific energy as $T \propto |\epsilon|^{-3/2}$, which means $|\epsilon| \propto T^{-2/3}$. 
Taking the derivative gives the relationship between energy intervals and period intervals: $d\epsilon \propto T^{-5/3} dT$.
Assuming the mass is uniformly distributed with respect to energy ($\frac{dM}{d\epsilon} = \text{constant}$), the mass return rate is:
$$\frac{dM}{dT} = \frac{dM}{d\epsilon} \left| \frac{d\epsilon}{dT} \right| \propto T^{-5/3}$$
Since the luminosity $L$ is proportional to the mass return rate at time $t = T$, we have $L \propto t^{-5/3}$.
**Value of $n$:** $5/3$

In this problem, we explore some of the design considerations for an electromagnet.

**a.** Consider an electromagnet consisting of a long solenoid, i.e. a spiral of thin wire wrapped in a single layer around a cylindrical nonmagnetic core. The wire is wrapped in such a way that the adjacent coils almost touch. When a current is sent through the wire, a magnetic field is generated inside the solenoid; this magnetic field exerts an outward force on the wire. Find the pressure $P$ on the solenoid in terms of the magnetic field $B$ inside the solenoid.

**b.** The pressure on the "walls" of the solenoid is counteracted by tension inside the wire. Derive an expression for the maximal achievable magnetic field $B$ in terms of coil radius $a$, wire diameter (thickness) $t \ll a$, and wire tensile strength $\sigma$. (The tensile strength of a material is the force per unit cross-sectional area that needs to be applied in order to pull the material apart.) Assume the wire is circular in cross-section.

**c.** Let $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $t = 0.001\text{ m}$. The tensile strength of copper is $\sigma = 250\text{ MPa}$, and the permeability of free space is $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}$. What is the maximum magnetic field that can be achieved in a single-layer solenoid made out of such a wire without the wire snapping?

**d.** In theory, we could generate a stronger field by increasing the wire thickness, but the nonuniform distribution of current inside the wire makes this difficult to analyze.
Instead, consider wrapping the solenoid in many layers of wire. We will place adjacent layers a distance $t$ apart so that they just barely don't touch, and will adjust the current through each wire to equalize the tensile stress. The wire coils span the space from an inner core radius of $a$ to an outer radius of $b$. Estimate the maximum achievable field strength inside this electromagnet. You may assume that the wire is thin ($t \ll a$, $t \ll b - a$).

**Part a**
When a current $I$ flows through the solenoid, it creates a uniform magnetic field $B$ inside and zero magnetic field outside. The solenoid can be modeled as a surface current density $K = nI$, where $n$ is the number of turns per unit length. By Ampere's law, $B = \mu_0 K$. 
The magnetic force per unit area (magnetic pressure) on the surface of the solenoid is given by the product of the surface current density and the average magnetic field across the current layer. Since the field drops from $B$ inside to $0$ outside, the average field is $B/2$.
$$P = K B_{\text{avg}} = \left(\frac{B}{\mu_0}\right) \left(\frac{B}{2}\right) = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$$

**Part b**
Consider a single turn of the wire, which forms a ring of radius $a$. The outward magnetic force per unit length on this wire is $f = I B_{\text{avg}} = I(B/2)$. 
The tension $T$ in a circular ring subjected to a uniform outward force per unit length $f$ is $T = fa$. Thus, the tension in the wire is:
$$T = I \frac{B}{2} a$$
Since the adjacent coils almost touch, the number of turns per unit length is $n = 1/t$. The magnetic field is $B = \mu_0 n I = \mu_0 I / t$, which means the current is $I = Bt/\mu_0$. Substituting this into the tension equation gives:
$$T = \left(\frac{Bt}{\mu_0}\right) \frac{B}{2} a = \frac{B^2 a t}{2\mu_0}$$
The maximum tension the wire can withstand before snapping is the tensile strength $\sigma$ multiplied by the cross-sectional area of the wire $A = \pi (t/2)^2 = \pi t^2 / 4$:
$$T_{\text{max}} = \sigma \frac{\pi t^2}{4}$$
Equating the magnetic tension to the maximum tension:
$$\frac{B^2 a t}{2\mu_0} = \sigma \frac{\pi t^2}{4} \implies B^2 = \frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma t}{2a}$$
$$B = \sqrt{\frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma t}{2a}}$$

**Part c**
We plug in the given values: $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $t = 0.001\text{ m}$, $\sigma = 250 \times 10^6\text{ Pa}$, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ H/m}$.
$$B = \sqrt{\frac{\pi (4\pi \times 10^{-7})(250 \times 10^6)(0.001)}{2(0.1)}} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2 (0.25)}{0.2}} = \sqrt{0.5\pi^2} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}$$
$$B \approx 2.22\text{ T}$$

**Part d**
In the multi-layer solenoid, the layers are spaced by $t$, so the number of layers per unit radial distance is $1/t$. The number of turns per unit length is also $1/t$. 
Let $B(r)$ be the magnetic field at radius $r$ and $I(r)$ be the current in the wire at that layer. By Ampere's law, the change in magnetic field across a radial thickness $dr$ is:
$$dB = -\mu_0 n I(r) (\text{number of layers}) = -\mu_0 \left(\frac{1}{t}\right) I(r) \left(\frac{dr}{t}\right) = -\frac{\mu_0 I(r)}{t^2} dr \implies I(r) = -\frac{t^2}{\mu_0} \frac{dB}{dr}$$
The tension in a wire at radius $r$ is $T(r) = I(r) B(r) r$. We adjust the current so that every wire is at the maximum tensile stress, $T(r) = \sigma \frac{\pi t^2}{4}$.
$$I(r) B(r) r = \sigma \frac{\pi t^2}{4}$$
Substitute $I(r)$ into the tension equation:
$$-\frac{t^2}{\mu_0} \frac{dB}{dr} B(r) r = \sigma \frac{\pi t^2}{4} \implies -B \, dB = \frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma}{4} \frac{dr}{r}$$
Integrate this from the inner radius $r = a$ (where $B = B_{\text{max}}$) to the outer radius $r = b$ (where $B = 0$):
$$\int_{B_{\text{max}}}^0 -B \, dB = \int_a^b \frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma}{4} \frac{dr}{r}$$
$$\left[ -\frac{1}{2}B^2 \right]_{B_{\text{max}}}^0 = \frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma}{4} \ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right) \implies \frac{1}{2}B_{\text{max}}^2 = \frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma}{4} \ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$$
$$B_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma}{2} \ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)}$$

**Part e**
Using the same material constants and $a = 0.1\text{ m}$, $b = 0.3\text{ m}$:
$$B_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi (4\pi \times 10^{-7})(250 \times 10^6)}{2} \ln\left(\frac{0.3}{0.1}\right)} = \sqrt{50\pi^2 \ln(3)}$$
$$B_{\text{max}} = \pi \sqrt{50 \ln(3)} \approx \pi \sqrt{50(1.0986)} \approx \pi \sqrt{54.93} \approx 23.3\text{ T}$$

Consider a disk with mass $m$ and radius $R$ placed on a large and frictionless table. An ant with mass $m$ is placed on top of the disk. The ant can move freely without sliding on the disk.

a. Initially, the ant starts on the edge of the disk, and both the ant and the disk are at rest (relative to the table). b. Suppose instead that the ant walks counterclockwise along the edge of the disk at constant speed $v$ in the frame of the disk. What is the ant's speed in the frame of the table?

c. Now there are two ants on the disk! The second ant (also of mass $m$) starts at distance $R/2$ from the center of the disk, with an angle offset by $\theta$ from the first ant. The second ant walks counterclockwise around this circle with radius $R/2$ at speed $v/2$ (relative to the disk). Find all $\theta$ such that the second ant is stationary in the frame of the table.

**Part a**
Let the velocity of the ant in the table frame be $v_a$ and the velocity of the disk in the table frame be $v_d$. Since the table is frictionless, the total momentum of the ant-disk system is conserved. Both start at rest, so the total momentum is zero:
$$m v_a + m v_d = 0 \implies v_d = -v_a$$
The velocity of the ant relative to the disk is $v$. Therefore, we can relate their velocities in the table frame:
$$v_a = v_d + v$$
Substituting $v_d = -v_a$ into the equation gives:
$$v_a = -v_a + v \implies 2v_a = v \implies v_a = \frac{v}{2}$$
Because the ant walks along the diameter, the force it exerts on the disk is purely radial (directed through the center of the disk). This means there is no torque on the disk about its center of mass, so the disk does not rotate ($\omega = 0$). Thus, the ant's velocity in the table frame is simply **$v/2$**.

**Part b**
Let the center of the disk be at $\vec{r}_d$ and the ant be at $\vec{r}_a$ in the table frame. The position of the ant relative to the disk center is $\vec{R} = \vec{r}_a - \vec{r}_d$, which has a constant magnitude $R$. 
By conservation of momentum, the center of mass of the system remains at the origin:
$$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{m\vec{r}_d + m\vec{r}_a}{2} = 0 \implies \vec{r}_d = -\frac{1}{2}\vec{R} \quad \text{and} \quad \vec{r}_a = \frac{1}{2}\vec{R}$$
Let $\omega$ be the angular velocity of the disk in the table frame. The ant walks at speed $v$ along the edge, so its angular velocity relative to the disk is $v/R$. The angular velocity of the vector $\vec{R}$ in the table frame is $\Omega = \omega + v/R$.
The velocities of the disk and the ant in the table frame are:
$$\vec{v}_d = \Omega \hat{k} \times \vec{r}_d \quad \text{and} \quad \vec{v}_a = \Omega \hat{k} \times \vec{r}_a$$
We now use conservation of angular momentum about the center of mass. The total angular momentum is the sum of the disk's spin angular momentum and the orbital angular momenta of the disk and the ant:
$$L = I\omega + m|\vec{r}_d|^2 \Omega + m|\vec{r}_a|^2 \Omega = 0$$
Substitute $I = \frac{1}{2}mR^2$ and $|\vec{r}_d| = |\vec{r}_a| = R/2$:
$$L = \frac{1}{2}mR^2\omega + m\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2 \Omega + m\left(\frac{R}{2}\right)^2 \Omega = \frac{1}{2}mR^2\omega + \frac{1}{2}mR^2\Omega = 0$$
This simplifies to $\omega + \Omega = 0$. Substituting $\Omega = \omega + v/R$ gives:
$$2\omega + \frac{v}{R} = 0 \implies \omega = -\frac{v}{2R} \implies \Omega = \frac{v}{2R}$$
The speed of the ant in the table frame is $v_a = |\vec{v}_a| = |\vec{r}_a| \Omega = \left(\frac{R}{2}\right) \left(\frac{v}{2R}\right) =$ **$v/4$**.

**Part c**
Let $\vec{R}_1$ and $\vec{R}_2$ be the position vectors of Ant 1 and Ant 2 relative to the disk center. Their magnitudes are $R$ and $R/2$, respectively. 
Ant 1 has an angular velocity of $v/R$ relative to the disk. Ant 2 walks at speed $v/2$ at a radius of $R/2$, so its angular velocity relative to the disk is also $(v/2)/(R/2) = v/R$. Because they share the same relative angular velocity, the angle $\theta$ between them remains constant, and both vectors $\vec{R}_1$ and $\vec{R}_2$ rotate at the same angular velocity $\Omega = \omega + v/R$ in the table frame.
The center of mass of the 3-mass system (disk + 2 ants) is stationary at the origin:
$$\vec{r}_{cm} = \frac{m\vec{r}_d + m(\vec{r}_d + \vec{R}_1) + m(\vec{r}_d + \vec{R}_2)}{3} = 0 \implies \vec{r}_d = -\frac{1}{3}(\vec{R}_1 + \vec{R}_2)$$
The position of Ant 2 in the table frame is:
$$\vec{r}_2 = \vec{r}_d + \vec{R}_2 = \frac{2}{3}\vec{R}_2 - \frac{1}{3}\vec{R}_1$$
For Ant 2 to be stationary in the table frame, its velocity $\vec{v}_2 = \Omega \hat{k} \times \vec{r}_2$ must be zero. 
By evaluating the total angular momentum of the system (similar to Part b), one can show that $\Omega = \frac{v}{2R} \frac{3}{4 - \cos\theta}$. Since $\cos\theta \le 1$, $\Omega$ is strictly positive and never zero. 
Therefore, for $\vec{v}_2 = 0$, we must have $\vec{r}_2 = 0$:
$$\frac{2}{3}\vec{R}_2 - \frac{1}{3}\vec{R}_1 = 0 \implies \vec{R}_1 = 2\vec{R}_2$$
Since $|\vec{R}_1| = R$ and $2|\vec{R}_2| = 2(R/2) = R$, the magnitudes already match. For the vectors to be equal, they must point in the exact same direction. Thus, the angle offset between the two ants must be **$0$**.

Problem B2: Where's the Kaboom?

A plane is flying horizontally at constant velocity $v$ and altitude $z = H$. The speed of sound at altitude $z$ is given by
$$c(z) = \alpha \sqrt{T(z)},$$
where $\alpha$ is a constant. Suppose $v > c(H)$, and define the Mach number as
$$M \equiv \frac{v}{c(H)} > 1.$$
If $c(z)$ is constant for all $z$, then the envelope is a cone with half angle $\theta$ where $\sin \theta = \frac{1}{M}$ and propagates with the speed of sound $c$.

a. Sketch the envelope.

b. Now, the speed of sound depends on the altitude because the temperature is not uniform. For the altitudes we are interested in, the following linear model works well:
$$T(z) = T_0 - \beta z,$$
where $\beta > 0$ is a constant. Sketch the envelope of the boom.

c. If the Mach number is large enough then the sonic boom hits the ground. Assume it is large enough. On the ground, there are two sensors at $z = 0$ and $z = h$, one directly above the other. Assume $h \ll H$ and $\beta h \ll T_0$. At time $t_1$, the top sensor receives the sonic boom signal and at a later time, the bottom sensor also receives the signal. Express the Mach number $M$ of the airplane in terms of $H, h, t, T_0, \alpha, \beta$, where $t = t_2 - t_1$.

d. If the plane travels slower without changing direction, its sonic boom could become no longer audible from the ground for the Mach number $1 < M < M_{\text{max}}$. What is the upper limit for the Mach number $M_{\text{max}}$ for which this can occur? Express your answer in terms of $T_0, H, \alpha, \beta$. You do not necessarily need all of these parameters.

c. $M = \left[ \left(1 - \frac{\beta H}{T_0}\right) \left(1 - \frac{\alpha^2 t^2 T_0}{h^2}\right) \right]^{-1/2}$

d. $M_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}}$

**Part a**
If the speed of sound $c(z)$ is constant, the envelope of the sonic boom is a perfect cone with its apex at the airplane, opening backwards along the flight path. The half-angle of this Mach cone is $\theta = \arcsin(1/M)$. 

**Part b**
With the temperature model $T(z) = T_0 - \beta z$ (where $\beta > 0$), the temperature and thus the speed of sound $c(z)$ increase as altitude $z$ decreases. Because sound travels faster at lower altitudes, the downward-propagating sound rays refract upwards (away from the normal) according to Snell's law. As a result, the envelope of the boom is a curved surface that bends forward, becoming steeper (more vertical) as it approaches the ground.

**Part c**
Let the shock wave surface be described by the arrival time $t_s(x, z)$. Since the airplane flies horizontally at a constant velocity $v$, the shock wave is stationary in the frame of the airplane, meaning $t_s(x, z) = \frac{x}{v} + f(z)$. 
The eikonal equation $|\nabla t_s| = 1/c(z)$ gives:
$$\sqrt{\frac{1}{v^2} + (f'(z))^2} = \frac{1}{c(z)} \implies f'(z) = -\sqrt{\frac{1}{c(z)^2} - \frac{1}{v^2}}$$
(We take the negative root because the wave propagates downwards, so arrival time increases as $z$ decreases).
For two sensors at the same horizontal position $x$, one at $z = h$ and one at $z = 0$, the time difference $t = t_2 - t_1$ is:
$$t = f(0) - f(h) \approx -h f'(0) = h \sqrt{\frac{1}{c(0)^2} - \frac{1}{v^2}}$$
We can rearrange this to solve for the airplane's velocity $v$:
$$\frac{t^2}{h^2} = \frac{1}{c(0)^2} - \frac{1}{v^2} \implies v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{c(0)^2} - \frac{t^2}{h^2}}}$$
The Mach number is defined as $M = \frac{v}{c(H)}$. Substituting $v$ into this definition gives:
$$M = \frac{1}{c(H) \sqrt{\frac{1}{c(0)^2} - \frac{t^2}{h^2}}}$$
Using the given speed of sound profile $c(z) = \alpha \sqrt{T_0 - \beta z}$, we have $c(0)^2 = \alpha^2 T_0$ and $c(H)^2 = \alpha^2 (T_0 - \beta H)$. Substituting these in yields:
$$M = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha^2 (T_0 - \beta H) \left( \frac{1}{\alpha^2 T_0} - \frac{t^2}{h^2} \right)}}$$
$$M = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(T_0 - \beta H) \left( \frac{1}{T_0} - \frac{\alpha^2 t^2}{h^2} \right)}}$$

**Part d**
For the sonic boom to reach the ground, the sound rays must not undergo total internal reflection before reaching $z = 0$. According to Snell's law, the horizontal trace velocity of the shock wave must be greater than or equal to the maximum speed of sound it encounters. 
Since $c(z)$ is maximized at the ground ($z = 0$), the condition for the boom to hit the ground is $v \ge c(0)$. 
If $v < c(0)$, the sound rays refract until they become horizontal and turn back upwards, making the boom inaudible on the ground. The upper limit for the Mach number where the boom is no longer audible corresponds to the critical velocity $v = c(0)$:
$$M_{\text{max}} = \frac{c(0)}{c(H)} = \frac{\alpha \sqrt{T_0}}{\alpha \sqrt{T_0 - \beta H}}$$
$$M_{\text{max}} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0}{T_0 - \beta H}}$$

**Problem B3: Locked and Moded**

a. Consider two mirrors facing each other separated by a distance $L$ (a Fabry–Pérot resonator). The cavity (the space between the two mirrors) is in vacuum (index of refraction $n = 1$, no dispersion), and the mirrors have high reflectivities so that the main resonance condition is that an integer multiple of half-wavelengths fit into the cavity. A light pulse containing multiple different frequencies travels between the mirrors and interferes with itself.
i. State the condition for resonance in terms of $L$ and wavelength $\lambda$.
ii. Write down an expression for the resonant angular frequencies $\omega_m$, with $m$ counting each of the possible resonances.
iii. What is the angular frequency spacing $\Delta\omega \equiv \omega_{m+1} - \omega_m$ between adjacent angular frequencies?

b. The electric field at the antinodes of the standing waves in the resonator is a superposition of oscillations at the resonant angular frequencies and is given by:
$$E_{\text{before}}(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} E_k \cos[(k \Delta\omega) t]$$
Now suppose we introduce a gain medium (such as a doped crystal) into the laser cavity. The gain medium completely absorbs incoming light and re-emits it over a finite range of $N$ angular frequencies centered around some angular frequency $\omega_0$, which coincides with one of the $\omega_m$ values determined above. Within this bandwidth, the gain medium amplifies and supports oscillations at all $\omega_m$ that fall within the range. (Assume $N$ is an odd number.)
Assume that each of these $N$ angular frequencies—also referred to as modes—has the same amplitude $E_0$, and that their phases are locked such that there is zero relative phase between them at $t = 0$. This condition is known as mode locking. Set their common phase so that all electric fields are expressed as cosine functions, consistent with the form of $E_{\text{before}}(t)$.
i. Write an expression for the total electric field $E_{\text{after}}(t)$ as the sum of these $N$ equally spaced angular frequencies (with zero relative phase).
ii. Show that in the limit of many angular frequencies ($\Delta\omega \ll \omega_0$, $N \gg 1$), the time-dependent electric field approximately takes the following form:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) \approx E_0 f(\omega_0, t) \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N (\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{(\Delta\omega) t}{2}\right)}$$
and determine the function $f(\omega_0, t)$.

c. To answer the next part of the problem, assume $N$ is odd and find the following limit when $a = \pi m$, where $m$ is an integer:
$$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}$$

d. Mode locking can dramatically increase the peak intensity $I$ of the laser output. Use the expression $I = \gamma E^2$, where $\gamma$ is a known constant, to answer the following questions.
i. Determine the total instantaneous intensity $I_{\text{after}}(t)$ of the electric field.
ii. What is the maximum possible intensity of the total field, and at what time(s) is this achieved?

e. The uncertainty principle states $\Delta x \Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$. In optics, we are more commonly interested in the duration of the pulse rather than its spatial extent; the two are related via $\Delta x = c \Delta t$. **Part a**
i. The condition for resonance in a Fabry-Pérot resonator is that an integer multiple of half-wavelengths must fit exactly into the cavity length $L$:
$$L = m \frac{\lambda}{2}$$
where $m = 1, 2, 3, \dots$

ii. The wavelength is related to the angular frequency by $\lambda = \frac{2\pi c}{\omega}$. Substituting this into the resonance condition gives $L = m \frac{\pi c}{\omega_m}$. Solving for $\omega_m$:
$$\omega_m = \frac{m \pi c}{L}$$

iii. The angular frequency spacing between adjacent modes is:
$$\Delta\omega = \omega_{m+1} - \omega_m = \frac{(m+1)\pi c}{L} - \frac{m\pi c}{L} = \frac{\pi c}{L}$$

**Part b**
i. The gain medium supports $N$ modes centered around $\omega_0$. Since $N$ is odd, we can index the modes by an integer $k$ ranging from $-(N-1)/2$ to $(N-1)/2$. The total electric field is the sum of these modes:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) = \sum_{k=-(N-1)/2}^{(N-1)/2} E_0 \cos[(\omega_0 + k \Delta\omega) t]$$

ii. We can evaluate this sum using the trigonometric identity for the sum of cosines with angles in arithmetic progression:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) = E_0 \sum_{k=-(N-1)/2}^{(N-1)/2} \left[ \cos(\omega_0 t)\cos(k \Delta\omega t) - \sin(\omega_0 t)\sin(k \Delta\omega t) \right]$$
Since sine is an odd function, the sine terms cancel out symmetrically. The cosine terms sum to:
$$E_{\text{after}}(t) = E_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N \Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}$$
Comparing this to the given form, we identify the function $f(\omega_0, t)$:
$$f(\omega_0, t) = \cos(\omega_0 t)$$

**Part c**
We want to find the limit $\lim_{x \to \pi m} \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x}$ for an integer $m$ and odd integer $N$. Using L'Hôpital's rule:
$$\lim_{x \to \pi m} \frac{\sin(Nx)}{\sin x} = \lim_{x \to \pi m} \frac{N \cos(Nx)}{\cos x} = \frac{N \cos(N\pi m)}{\cos(\pi m)}$$
Since $N$ is odd, $N\pi m$ and $\pi m$ are either both even multiples of $\pi$ (if $m$ is even) or both odd multiples of $\pi$ (if $m$ is odd). Therefore, $\cos(N\pi m)$ and $\cos(\pi m)$ are either both $1$ or both $-1$. In either case, their ratio is $1$, so the limit is:
$$N$$

**Part d**
i. The total instantaneous intensity is $I_{\text{after}}(t) = \gamma E_{\text{after}}(t)^2$:
$$I_{\text{after}}(t) = \gamma E_0^2 \cos^2(\omega_0 t) \left( \frac{\sin\left(\frac{N \Delta\omega t}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2}\right)} \right)^2$$

ii. The maximum value of the fraction squared is $N^2$, which occurs when the denominator goes to zero, i.e., when $\frac{\Delta\omega t}{2} = \pi m'$ for some integer $m'$. At these times, $t = \frac{2\pi m'}{\Delta\omega}$. 
Because $\omega_0$ is a resonant frequency, it is an integer multiple of $\Delta\omega$ (i.e., $\omega_0 = m_0 \Delta\omega$). Thus, at these times, $\omega_0 t = m_0 \Delta\omega \left(\frac{2\pi m'}{\Delta\omega}\right) = 2\pi m_0 m'$, which means $\cos^2(\omega_0 t) = 1$.
The maximum possible intensity is:
$$I_{\text{max}} = \gamma E_0^2 N^2$$
This is achieved at times:
$$t = \frac{2\pi m'}{\Delta\omega} \quad \text{for any integer } m'$$

**Part e**
Using the de Broglie relation $p = \frac{\hbar \omega}{c}$, the uncertainty in momentum is $\Delta p = \frac{\hbar}{c} \Delta\omega$. The spatial extent of the pulse is related to its duration by $\Delta x = c \Delta t$. Substituting these into the uncertainty principle $\Delta x \Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$:
$$(c \Delta t) \left(\frac{\hbar}{c} \Delta\omega\right) \ge \frac{\hbar}{2} \implies \Delta\omega \Delta t \ge \frac{1}{2}$$
Thus, the required bandwidth to achieve a pulse of duration $\Delta t$ is $\Delta\omega \ge \frac{1}{2\Delta t}$.

In our mode-locked laser, the total gain bandwidth is $\Delta\omega_{\text{gain}} = N \Delta\omega$. The duration of the pulse $\Delta t$ can be estimated by the width of the main intensity peak, which is the time from the peak maximum to its first zero. The first zero occurs when $\frac{N \Delta\omega t}{2} = \pi$, giving a pulse duration of $\Delta t \approx \frac{2\pi}{N \Delta\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{\Delta\omega_{\text{gain}}}$.
Multiplying the two gives $\Delta\omega_{\text{gain}} \Delta t \approx 2\pi$. This shows that the mode-locked laser achieves a pulse duration that is inversely proportional to the gain bandwidth, which is on the same order of magnitude as the theoretical minimum allowed by the uncertainty principle (a transform-limited pulse).
